questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: Why old-fashioned idioms are better than new ones
How sports have changed the English language
New idioms and where they come from
Why young people don't use idioms any more
questions.why: Sam says they'll learn modern idioms that have come into English through the internet, TV and social media.

questions.q: Why is Rob confused at the start of the programme?
options: He thinks Sam wants to go shopping
He thinks Sam wants to borrow some money
He doesn't know that the programme has started
He can't hear what Sam is saying
questions.why: When Sam says she has to 'spend a penny', Rob asks, 'You're going shopping now, are you?'

questions.q: What does Rob think about the phrase 'spend a penny'?
options: It is a new phrase that came from social media
It is still used by most young people today
It is only used in very formal situations
It is old, and young people wouldn't know it
questions.why: Rob says Sam is 'showing her age' and most young people today wouldn't know what it meant.

questions.q: Why did Dr Gareth Carrol become interested in modern idioms?
options: He wanted to write a book about famous films
He didn't know many phrases his students used
His students asked him to explain old idioms
He was asked to teach a course on social media
questions.why: Sam says he realised he didn't know many of the expressions his students used in everyday speech.

questions.q: What surprised Gareth Carrol about the phrase 'Groundhog Day'?
options: Very few people used it in everyday speech
It had a completely different meaning in the film
Some students knew it but not that it was a film
It was invented by one of his students
questions.why: He says a number of students knew the phrase but 'had no idea it was a film'.

questions.q: What does Michael Rosen say about the phrase 'go viral'?
options: It has now completely disappeared from use
It was first used in a famous film
It is only used by doctors and scientists
It came early in the internet age and stayed
questions.why: Michael Rosen says, 'In the early days we had go viral which has stayed with us.'

questions.q: According to Gareth Carrol, where did 'first-world problems' begin?
options: As a hashtag on Twitter
In a popular TV comedy
In a newspaper article
In a famous movie title
questions.why: He says the phrase 'started life as Twitter hashtag'.

questions.q: Why does Rob tell listeners not to worry if they don't know these idioms?
options: Because most of these idioms will soon disappear
Native speakers only fully know idioms at 30 to 40
Because idioms are never used in exams or at work
Because the classic idioms are no longer used
questions.why: He says a native speaker's full knowledge of idioms develops at around the age of thirty to forty.
